correctness.rationale: From positive goods and m>=n EF1 loads are positive integers with spread at most two; pair smoothing needs at most floor(n/2) steps of multiplier at most 4/3; balanced integer product upper-bounds optimum. The explicitly constructed EF1 and all-utility-two allocations attain equality. A separate exact enumeration checked 6497 finite allocation count vectors.

evidence: Yang et al. prove exact Nash optimality for uniform goods and epsilon-small-good ratios depending on epsilon.
Barman et al. present general approximate Nash guarantees for fair allocations.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Uniform-valued exact optimality is a strict subfamily; the small-item result has additional size-relative-to-average conditions and does not supply this exact uniform bound across all m>=n. Broad generic bounds are weaker and their application does not subsume sharpness.

evidence: arxiv:2609.03846, abstract and theoretical results: universal e^{-1/e}, uniform-value 1, small-item epsilon-dependent bound.
Earlier literature establishes existence of efficient EF1 and other allocation properties, not all-EF1 sharp positive-bivalued ratio in the inspected material.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: An exact guarantee for all EF1 allocations is logically distinct from the EF1 property of a welfare optimum or an algorithm constructing one fair allocation. The result can be derived from the spread property plus new discrete-product analysis, but was not found as an existing implication with the sharp constant and equality examples in the inspected texts.

evidence: arxiv:2609.03846, Sections 3.2–3.3 and its bounded-spread argument

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Equivalent product language, positive-bivalued language, and exact fraction language were compared. An EF1 spread-of-two lemma alone does not imply the sharp finite-agent ratio without controlling the count of simultaneous extremal pairs and proving attainability; the new proof supplies both.

exact_database_or_table.reasoning: No relevant published exact table was located among reviewed results. The claim is a closed-form all-n theorem, not a transcription of finite tabular values; missing search hits cannot establish exclusivity.

originality.rationale: The motivating 2026 source gives a uniform-value result and a different small-item bound, rather than the inspected sharp {a,2a} guarantee for all inventories and n. Earlier welfare papers give broader approximate ratios without this matching finite-n guarantee. Literature and semantic overlap searches found no exact equivalent, subject to unindexed-priority risk.
residual_risks: A mathematically equivalent bivalued EF1 ratio may exist in unindexed literature.

value.rationale: An exact worst-case welfare retention factor for every EF1 allocation across all inventories in the basic strictly positive two-value class addresses the 2026 motivating paper’s quality-of-arbitrary-fair-allocation question. Both a universal proof and for-every-n equality construction show the precise cost of fair but nonoptimal output rather than a small numerical gain.
